evidence.quote: rocky lowlands, mixed-grass prairie and cross timbers.

evidence.quote: From iconic animals such as bison (buffalo)

evidence.claim: The Wichita Mountains Byway winds through rocky lowlands, mixed-grass prairie and cross timbers, linking historic communities with the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge.
evidence.quote: A traveler along the Wichita Mountains Scenic Byway will be met with an awe-inspiring mosaic of rocky lowlands, mixed-grass prairie and cross timbers.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration identifies it as a National Scenic Byway and allows at least two hours.
evidence.quote: National Scenic Byway • Oklahoma Length 93.0 mi / 149.7 km Time to Allow at least 2 hours

evidence.claim: Oklahoma’s tourism department emphasizes wildlife viewing, including bison, along a route through the refuge.
evidence.quote: The Wichita Mountains Scenic Byway offers many great wildlife viewing opportunities, especially as the route passes through the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge.

evidence.claim: The protected landscape took shape in stages. A forest preserve was proclaimed in 1901, and Theodore Roosevelt established a game preserve for bison in 1905.
evidence.quote: In 1901, this area was proclaimed a “Forest Preserve,” and then in 1905 President Theodore Roosevelt created the first “Game Preserve” at the Wichita Mountains for the nearly-extinct bison.

evidence.claim: Fifteen bison arrived from the Bronx Zoo in 1907.
evidence.quote: descendants of the original 15 transported from the Bronx Zoo in 1907.

evidence.claim: In 1936, the forest designation ended, administration passed to the Bureau of Biological Survey, and the land became the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge.
evidence.quote: On June 4, 1936, the Wichita Forest designation was abolished and transferred to the Bureau of Biological Survey, a precursor to the Fish and Wildlife Service. It was re-designated the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge (WMWR).

evidence.claim: The byway branches west of Apache. Highway 19 reaches Highway 58, which runs north to Carnegie and south toward Medicine Park.
evidence.quote: The Wichita Mountains Scenic Byway is identified as beginning at Apache and extending west on Hwy 19 to the Hwy 58/19 junction. The byway then proceeds north and south on Hwy 58 to Carnegie in the north and Medicine Park in the south.

evidence.claim: On the northern circuit, Highway 9 extends west from Carnegie to Mountain View, while Highway 115 leads south toward Highway 49.
evidence.quote: From Carnegie, the byway proceeds west on Hwy 9 to Mountain View and south on Hwy 115 to the junction of Hwy 49 and Hwy 115.

evidence.claim: Meers stands on Highway 115 in the foothills.
evidence.quote: Meers is an unincorporated community located on State Highway 115 in Comanche County, Oklahoma, United States, in the foothills of the Wichita Mountains.

evidence.claim: Highway 49 crosses the refuge, reaching Medicine Park and continuing east to I-44.
evidence.quote: From Medicine Park in the south, the byway extends east on Hwy 49 to I-44 and west on Hwy 49 through the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge.

evidence.claim: linking historic communities
evidence.quote: the road winds through low impact landscapes and historic communities.

evidence.claim: Meers began in 1901 as a gold-prospecting town, named for mine operator Andrew J. Meers.
evidence.quote: In 1901, Meers was founded as a gold prospecting town where it was named in honor of mine operator Andrew J. Meers from Cherokee County, Georgia.

evidence.claim: Its surviving original structure is the Meers Store & Restaurant.
evidence.quote: The only remaining structure of the original town is the Meers Store & Restaurant

evidence.claim: The store served as the area post office from March 1902 until February 1989.
evidence.quote: The Meers Store also served as the area post office from March 12, 1902, until February, 1989.

evidence.claim: In 1978 it entered the National Register as Meers Mining Camp, recognizing the surviving remnant of the gold-rush community.
evidence.quote: The Meers Store was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978 as Meers Mining Camp, since it was the only surviving relic of the community's gold rush days.

evidence.claim: The Oklahoma Geological Survey installed a seismograph in the store in 1985 to monitor seismic activity.
evidence.quote: In 1985, in order to monitor a seismic event, the Oklahoma Geological Survey installed a seismograph in the Meers Store.

evidence.claim: A paved road winds three miles up Mount Scott to a summit 2,464 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: Visitors can reach the summit by car or bicycle via a three-mile paved road.

evidence.claim: The climb includes steep grades, sharp turns and scenic pullouts.
evidence.quote: Several scenic pullouts are located along the road

evidence.claim: From the mountain’s western side, the view includes Elk Mountain and Mount Sheridan.
evidence.quote: From the west side of Mount Scott, several prominent mountains can be seen to the west including Elk Mountain, Mount Sheridan

evidence.claim: North of Mount Scott, Blue Canyon Wind Farm’s turbines are visible from the access road.
evidence.quote: The Blue Canyon Wind Farm is north of Mount Scott, and the wind turbines are visible from the access road.

evidence.claim: The peak is named for General Winfield Scott.
evidence.quote: The peak was named in honor of General Winfield Scott.

evidence.claim: The refuge’s mountains rise 800 to 1,000 feet above the surrounding prairie, but their slopes are steep and rocky.
evidence.quote: Although the mountains rise only 800 to 1000 feet above the surrounding prairie, they are steep and rocky.

evidence.claim: Wind turbines at Blue Canyon Wind Farm are visible north of Mount Scott from the access road.
evidence.quote: The Blue Canyon Wind Farm is north of Mount Scott, and the wind turbines are visible from the access road.

evidence.claim: 2,464 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: rising to a height of 2,464 feet (751 m)

evidence.claim: steep grades, sharp turns
evidence.quote: due to the steep grades, heavy crosswinds, and sharp turns.

evidence.claim: Red granite cobblestones give many of Medicine Park’s original buildings their material character.
evidence.quote: Many of the original structures are constructed of naturally formed cobblestones—these red granite cobblestones are unique to the Wichita Mountains.

evidence.claim: Elmer Thomas, then an Oklahoma state senator, founded the resort town on July 4, 1908.
evidence.quote: Medicine Park was founded on July 4, 1908, by Elmer Thomas, a young lawyer who had just become a member of the Oklahoma State Senate

evidence.claim: Its first meal service occupied a surplus Army tent with a wooden floor.
evidence.quote: When the resort first opened, it consisted merely of a large surplus Army tent with a wooden floor where hot meals were served.

evidence.claim: Two dams on Medicine Creek formed Bath Lake Swimming Hole, with a small number of campsites alongside the early resort.
evidence.quote: Two dams were constructed on Medicine Creek to form Bath Lake Swimming Hole, and a limited number of campsites were constructed.

evidence.claim: Visitors came from Oklahoma and North Texas; two inns followed, the Outside Inn and Apache Inn.
evidence.quote: Tourists came to Medicine Park from around Oklahoma and North Texas. Soon, there were two inns—the Outside Inn and the Apache Inn.

evidence.claim: Many original buildings use the Wichita Mountains’ naturally formed red granite cobblestones.
evidence.quote: Many of the original structures are constructed of naturally formed cobblestones—these red granite cobblestones are unique to the Wichita Mountains.

evidence.claim: TravelOK describes wildflowers in the warmer months and autumn color in both trees and grasses.
evidence.quote: Guests during the warmer months will be met with an explosion of color from countless wildflowers. In the fall, visitors are greeted with the changing colors of autumn from the trees to the various grasses.

evidence.claim: Within the refuge, steep, rocky mountains rise 800 to 1,000 feet above the surrounding prairie.
evidence.quote: Although the mountains rise only 800 to 1000 feet above the surrounding prairie, they are steep and rocky.

evidence.claim: The community lies at the Meers Fault, a fracture in the ground with northwestern and southeastern sections.
evidence.quote: Meers is defined by a geological displacement or planar fracture known as the Meers Fault. The northwestern Meers fault and the southeastern Meers fault lines are geologically situated in the central lowlands.

evidence.claim: The climb ends at a parking area on top of the mountain.
evidence.quote: parking is available at the top of the mountain.

evidence.claim: The Dance Hall later drew Bob Wills and The Texas Playboys as regular performers from 1929 through the late 1930s.
evidence.quote: Bob Wills and The Texas Playboys became regulars at the Dance Hall from 1929 through the late 1930s.

flags: No cache page supplies byway construction or campaign history. The overview uses the documented forest-preserve, game-preserve and wildlife-refuge sequence without treating them as the same designation.
Dropped the current unqualified oldest-refuge claim: the cache says oldest managed wildlife facility, and FHWA says one of the oldest managed nature preserves. Those are different categories.

Mountain-age claims vary: approximately 500 million years in Wikipedia versus 550 million in FHWA, with a separate 290–330 million-year uplift date. No geological source is cached; numeric age omitted.

The corridor is a branching network. The strip towns are not in ascending mile order and catalog mileage differs from FHWA’s 93 miles. Used the tourism department’s network description; moments retain the established Meers, Mount Scott, Medicine Park sequence for a southbound/eastbound refuge visit. A single uninterrupted loop is not asserted.

Mount Scott page contradicts itself on pedestrian and cycling hours and on highest-peak rankings. Omitted hours, rankings and guaranteed access; no refuge-manager page is cached. Current artillery-sound detail is supported but omitted to focus on visible terrain.
Meers remains a town-history moment. Its store qualifies as a historic landmark in the cache, listed as Meers Mining Camp; no restaurant promotion or present service claim is included.
